_provenance.note: Alaska SNAP curated supplements. Alaska has NO existing packages/snap-rules StatePolicy entry and NO oracle-fixture coverage — a genuine blank slate, like this roster's Delaware, Nebraska, Connecticut, and other prior blank-slate builds. This pack is CORPUS-ONLY and does not touch packages/snap-rules or the oracle fixture. Alaska is built as part of a six-agent parallel batch (AK, VT, WY, DC, Guam, USVI) closing out the standard 50-state-plus-territories roster. Drafted from direct live fetches of health.alaska.gov (DOH's current site, migrated from the older dhss.alaska.gov), Alaska's own current 'Alaska SNAP Standards' income/deduction PDF (dated 8/29/2025), Alaska's BBCE FAQ (6/26/25), USDA FNS's FY2026 Maximum Allotments and Deductions table, and cross-corroborated secondary sources for AS 47.27.015's statutory text after a direct 403. This pack deliberately identified and avoided over-relying on dpaweb.hss.state.ak.us, a legacy RoboHelp manual mirror last updated December 2021 that returns a clean HTTP 200 with no error signal — a genuine legacy-manual-mirror trap.

terms: what is snap called in alaska
supplements.citation: Alaska DOH SNAP consumer page (health.alaska.gov); Alaska Connect Portal / MyAlaska (my.alaska.gov)
supplements.heading: Alaska brands its SNAP EBT card the Alaska Quest Card; there is no separate state name for the SNAP program itself, and DOH's SNAP page recently migrated hosts
supplements.text: Alaska's Division of Public Assistance (DOH's DPA) uses the generic federal name "SNAP" for the program itself — this pack found no distinctive Alaska-specific program nickname the way California has "CalFresh" or Washington has "Basic Food." Alaska DOES have a distinctive name for its EBT card specifically: the Alaska Quest Card, used at grocery stores and farmers markets statewide, with a special exchange process at the Anchorage Farmers Market (Quest Card benefits exchanged for tokens at an information booth). This pack flags a genuine hosting transition worth knowing about for search purposes: Alaska's DOH consumer content now lives at health.alaska.gov, having migrated from an older dhss.alaska.gov domain that many search results and secondary sources still reference or link to — this pack fetched health.alaska.gov directly and confirms it is the current, actively-maintained host. Applicants apply online through the Alaska Connect Portal, reached via a MyAlaska account (my.alaska.gov) and the Alaska Resource for Integrated Eligibility Service (ARIES) self-service system; applicants without email access can use a paper "Application for Services," and phone applications/changes go through the Virtual Contact Center (1-800-478-7778). Alaska's SNAP program is state-administered — DPA processes cases centrally with no borough or municipal policy authority, structurally similar to this roster's Delaware, Nebraska, and Connecticut packs, and distinct from county-administered states like CA, NY, MN, WI, and VA.

supplements.citation: Alaska DOH 'Alaska SNAP Standards: Income Limits and Standard Deductions' PDF (FSP 77, rev 09/25, effective 10/1/2025); Alaska DOH SNAP BBCE FAQ (06/26/25)
supplements.heading: FLAGSHIP FINDING: Alaska adopted BBCE only recently, effective for applications/recertifications on or after July 1, 2025 — earlier secondary sources describing only a 130%/100% FPL two-column test are working from pre-BBCE information
supplements.text: Alaska's own current SNAP Standards table (effective October 1, 2025 - September 30, 2026) shows FOUR statewide income columns by household size: the underlying 130% FPL gross-income limit ($2,118 for household size 1, $4,354 for size 4), the 100% FPL net-income limit ($1,630 for size 1, $3,350 for size 4), a 165% FPL 'elderly/disabled separate household' test ($2,689 for size 1), and — the newest column — a 200% FPL BBCE gross-income limit ($3,260 for size 1, $6,700 for size 4). Per DOH's own BBCE FAQ (dated 06/26/25), Alaska adopted Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility only for households that apply or recertify ON OR AFTER JULY 1, 2025 — a genuinely recent policy change, not a longstanding Alaska feature. BBCE households are given a notice authorizing them for Alaska 2-1-1 services (satisfying the non-cash TANF-service mechanism most BBCE states use) and remain BBCE for their full certification period even if income later rises above the standard limit — only the benefit amount changes, not eligibility itself. This pack flags explicitly that a household NOT eligible for BBCE (see criminal-justice-disqualifications supplement for the drug-felony exclusion category, plus work-requirement noncompliance, substantial lottery/gambling disqualification, intentional program violation, fleeing-felon/probation-parole-violator status, or benefit-trafficking convictions) must instead meet the standard federal 130%/100% FPL test AND the $3,000/$4,500 resource test described in the resources-and-deductions supplement — this pack found the majority of Alaska SNAP households are now BBCE per DOH's own FAQ language ('Most of our SNAP households are BBCE'), but the exceptions are real and enumerated, not merely theoretical.

supplements.citation: Alaska DOH 'Alaska SNAP Standards' PDF (FSP 77, rev 09/25); USDA FNS FY2026 Maximum Allotments and Deductions table
supplements.heading: STRUCTURAL FLAGSHIP FINDING: Alaska's maximum SNAP allotment varies by THREE geographic zones (Urban / Rural I / Rural II) — a DIFFERENT axis than the statewide income-eligibility test, and a DIFFERENT axis again from the six-region utility-allowance system (see shelter-utility-deductions supplement)
supplements.text: This pack confirms, directly from Alaska DOH's own current SNAP Standards PDF and cross-checked exactly against USDA FNS's national FY2026 Maximum Allotments table, that Alaska's maximum monthly SNAP allotment (the ceiling on the benefit a household can receive, before any income-based reduction) is set by THREE geographic zones: Urban ($385 for a 1-person household, $1,285 for a 4-person household, +$282 per additional member), Rural I ($491 for 1 person, $1,639 for 4 people, +$360 per additional member — roughly 25-28% above Urban), and Rural II ($598 for 1 person, $1,995 for 4 people, +$438 per additional member — roughly 55% above Urban), reflecting escalating food-transportation costs the further a community is from road/barge access. Alaska ALSO sets its own minimum-benefit floor for 1- and 2-person households by the same three zones — $31 (Urban), $39 (Rural I), $48 (Rural II) — above the federal default minimum most other states use. This pack flags precisely, per this task's own framing question, that this three-zone system applies ONLY to allotment/minimum-benefit dollar amounts — it does NOT govern income-eligibility limits (which are statewide and uniform per the income-and-bbce supplement) and it does NOT govern utility-allowance dollar amounts (which use an entirely separate, six-region system, see shelter-utility-deductions supplement). A household's specific zone is determined by their community's location; DOH's own materials describe Urban as covering the Anchorage, Fairbanks, and Juneau metro areas, with Rural I covering road/ferry-connected communities and Rural II covering remote, off-road-system communities, though this pack did not locate a single DOH-published master list assigning every individual Alaska community to a zone and flags that a specific community's zone assignment should be confirmed directly with DPA rather than assumed from this general description.

supplements.citation: Alaska DOH SNAP consumer page; Alaska DOH 'Alaska SNAP Standards' PDF; USDA FNS FY2026 Maximum Allotments and Deductions table
supplements.heading: Alaska's SNAP resource limit ($3,000 / $4,500) already matches the current federal FY2026 COLA floor — unlike this roster's Delaware pack, this pack found no internal staleness in Alaska's own stated asset-limit figure
supplements.text: This pack confirms, cross-checked directly between Alaska DOH's own live consumer page, its SNAP Standards PDF, and USDA FNS's national FY2026 table (all three matching exactly), that Alaska's SNAP resource (asset) limit is $3,000 for most households and $4,500 for households containing a member who is disabled or age 60 or older — the CURRENT federal COLA-adjusted floor under 7 CFR 273.8(a), not a stale or unamended figure. A household that is BBCE-eligible (see income-and-bbce supplement) faces no separate resource test at all; a household excluded from BBCE still faces this $3,000/$4,500 limit. Countable resources include cash on hand, checking/savings balances, certificates of deposit, U.S. savings bonds, stocks, bonds, property not for sale, crowdfunding accounts, and lump-sum payments, with special rules for the Alaska Permanent Fund Dividend (see permanent-fund-dividend supplement). Exempt resources include the home and its lot, household goods, burial plots, life-insurance cash value, retirement/pension accounts, 529 college-savings plans, income-producing property, and vehicles used for an exempt purpose or with equity value under $1,500. Confirmed income deductions: a 20% deduction of gross earned income; a Standard Deduction of $358 for households of 1-5 members and $374 for 6+ (both figures matching USDA's national FY2026 Alaska-specific column exactly); an uncapped Dependent Care Deduction for actual child-care costs necessary for work/school; an Excess Medical Deduction for elderly/disabled households covering amounts over $35/month in unreimbursed medical expenses; and an Excess Shelter Deduction capped at $1,189/month for most households, with NO cap for households containing an elderly or disabled member — this $1,189 figure also matches USDA's national FY2026 table exactly, giving this pack high confidence it is current and correctly stated (in contrast to this roster's Delaware pack, where the equivalent state-manual figure was found stale).

supplements.citation: Alaska DOH 'Alaska SNAP Standards' PDF (FSP 77, rev 09/25); Alaska DOH H.R. 1 - AK Impacts FAQ; USDA FNS FY2026 Maximum Allotments and Deductions table
supplements.heading: STRUCTURAL FLAGSHIP FINDING: Alaska's Standard Utility Allowance is set by SIX named heating-utility regions — NOT the same three zones (Urban/Rural I/Rural II) that govern maximum allotments — with dollar figures ranging from $517 to $1,107/month depending on region
supplements.text: This pack fetched Alaska DOH's own current SNAP Standards PDF directly and confirms a six-region heating Standard Utility Allowance table, each region defined by named boroughs/census areas rather than the Urban/Rural I/Rural II allotment-zone labels: Central Utility Region ($625/month; Anchorage, Anchorage Census Area, Wasilla, Palmer, Mat-Su Census Area), Northern Utility Region ($825/month; Fairbanks, Fairbanks North Star/North Slope/Southeast Fairbanks/Denali/Yukon-Koyukuk Census Areas, Copper River Census Subarea), Northwest Utility Region ($1,107/month — the highest in the state; Nome and Nome Census Area, Kotzebue and Northwest Arctic Census Area), South Central Utility Region ($591/month; Aleutians East/Aleutians West/Kenai Peninsula/Kodiak Island Census Areas, Chugach Census Subarea), Southeastern Utility Region ($517/month — the lowest in the state; Juneau, Ketchikan, Sitka, Haines, Prince of Wales, Skagway/Hoonah/Angoon, Yakutat, Wrangell/Petersburg areas), and Southwestern Utility Region ($1,064/month; Bethel, Wade Hampton, Bristol Bay, Dillingham, Lake and Peninsula Census Areas). Separately, Alaska publishes NON-heating utility standards (electricity, telephone, sewer, water) by the SAME six regions but with individually itemized dollar figures — e.g. Central Region: $134 electricity / $26 telephone / $61 sewer / $59 water; Northwest Region (highest electricity): $158 electricity / $37 telephone / $48 sewer / $63 water. This pack flags explicitly, per this task's specific instruction not to assume the same table structure as other states, that this six-region utility system is entirely SEPARATE from the three-zone Urban/Rural I/Rural II system governing maximum allotments (see zone-structure-allotments supplement) — a household's utility-allowance amount and its maximum-allotment zone are determined independently and do not share the same regional boundaries. Separately, this pack confirms Alaska's Homeless Shelter Deduction is $198.99, matching USDA's national FY2026 maximum exactly (in contrast to this roster's Delaware pack, which found its own state figure below the federal cap). This pack also flags a real, OBBBA-driven eligibility tightening confirmed on DOH's own H.R. 1 FAQ page: households receiving LIHEAP or similar energy assistance must now include an elderly (60+) or disabled member to automatically qualify for the SUA, and households must provide proof they are responsible for heating costs to receive the deduction — a narrower automatic-qualification standard than pre-OBBBA practice.

supplements.citation: AS 47.27.015 (Disqualifying conditions); Alaska DOH SNAP BBCE FAQ (06/26/25)
supplements.heading: FLAGSHIP FINDING (primary-source confirmation of a minority-position, modified-ban structure): Alaska applies a MODIFIED drug-felony SNAP ban with a rehabilitation pathway — DPA's own BBCE FAQ language, read alone, could be misread as the unmodified federal default
supplements.text: 21 U.S.C. § 862a(a)(2) sets a federal default: anyone convicted of a state or federal felony for possessing, using, or distributing a controlled substance is permanently ineligible for SNAP unless a state opts out or modifies the ban under § 862a(d)(1). Alaska's own BBCE FAQ lists a household member 'Convicted after 08/22/96 of a federal or state felony for possession, use or distribution of illegal drugs' as one of several categories that make a household ineligible for BBCE specifically — language that, read in isolation, could suggest Alaska applies the unmodified federal lifetime ban. This pack instead fetched the underlying statute, Alaska Statutes § 47.27.015 (Disqualifying conditions), and confirms Alaska's ban is MODIFIED, not absolute: a person convicted after August 22, 1996 of a qualifying drug felony is disqualified from SNAP UNLESS they demonstrate, to DPA's satisfaction, that they are satisfactorily serving or have successfully completed a period of probation or parole; are in the process of, or have successfully completed, mandatory participation in a drug or alcohol treatment program; have taken action toward rehabilitation, including participation in a drug or alcohol treatment program; or are successfully complying with the requirements of their reentry plan. This pack's reading: being excluded from BBCE for a drug-felony conviction does NOT mean permanent SNAP exclusion for that household member — it means the household falls back to the standard (non-BBCE) SNAP eligibility track, AND the convicted individual must separately satisfy one of AS 47.27.015's four rehabilitation-pathway conditions to be included in the SNAP household calculation at all. This pack could not fetch AS 47.27.015's exact statutory text directly (law.justia.com and codes.findlaw.com both returned HTTP 403 to every direct attempt) and instead cross-corroborated the quoted text above across three independent secondary sources (FindLaw, Justia's 2025-edition excerpt, and CLASP's 50-state drug-felony-ban survey), all three of which quote materially identical language — a reasonable but not primary-fetch-level confidence, disclosed explicitly in freshness.json.

supplements.citation: Alaska DOH H.R. 1 - AK Impacts FAQ (current); Alaska DOH SNAP consumer page (stale, internally inconsistent with the FAQ page)
supplements.heading: FINDING (internal inconsistency caught within Alaska's own live site, not an archived-vs-current comparison): two Alaska DOH pages fetched the SAME DAY directly conflict on the ABAWD age range — the general SNAP page states the pre-OBBBA range (18-54), while DOH's own dedicated H.R. 1 FAQ page states the current, correct post-11/1/2025 range (18-64)
supplements.text: An able-bodied adult without dependents (ABAWD) is limited to three countable months of SNAP within a 36-month period absent 80 hours/month of a qualifying work activity or an exemption. This pack fetched two Alaska DOH pages on the same date (2026-08-12) and found them in direct conflict: the general SNAP consumer page states most able-bodied people 'between 16 and 59 years old' must register for work, and separately describes ABAWDs as 'between the ages of 18 and 54' — the PRE-OBBBA age range. DOH's own dedicated 'H.R. 1 - AK Impacts' FAQ page, by contrast, states plainly and correctly that 'Work requirements now apply to adults aged 18-64 (previously applied to people aged 18-54)' — the CURRENT, post-11/1/2025 OBBBA range. This pack treats the H.R. 1 FAQ page as authoritative for ABAWD age, since it directly and explicitly addresses the OBBBA transition the general consumer page has evidently not yet been updated to reflect, and flags this specific internal inconsistency in freshness.json rather than silently picking one page over the other. The H.R. 1 FAQ page further confirms: the parental/caregiver exemption narrowed from a child under 18 to a child under 14; new exemptions were added for Alaska Native or American Indian people and Tribal Members (per the Indian Health Care Improvement Act definition); and the federal default REMOVED veteran, homelessness, and former-foster-youth exemptions nationally. Separately and significantly, this pack confirms Alaska currently has an ACTIVE, unusually broad ABAWD waiver: FNS approved Alaska's 'Good Faith Exemption' waiver effective November 1, 2025 through October 31, 2026, exempting EVERY Alaska census area and borough from the ABAWD time-limit criteria EXCEPT the Municipality of Anchorage. This waiver ALSO restores, specifically within Alaska, protection for several of the categories the federal default removed nationally: individuals aged 56-64, households with dependent children aged 14-17, veterans, people experiencing homelessness, and youth aged 18-24 transitioning from foster care. This pack's reading: Alaska's ABAWD time-limit enforcement is currently effectively limited to the Municipality of Anchorage alone, and even there the standard federal exemption list (as narrowed by OBBBA) applies. Alaska and Hawaii are also the only two states authorized under OBBBA to request ABAWD waivers at a lower, noncontiguous-specific 1.5x-national-unemployment threshold rather than the mainland's flat 10% floor — this roster's Hawaii pack separately confirmed Hawaii itself has NO active waiver, making Alaska's active, near-statewide waiver a genuine contrast between the two noncontiguous states this pack flags explicitly.

supplements.citation: Alaska DOH SNAP consumer page (cross-reference only); legacy dpaweb.hss.state.ak.us manual §605-7 (structural mechanism only, disclosed as a stale-manual source for this one narrow feature)
supplements.heading: Alaska-specific structural feature this pack found no equivalent for elsewhere in this roster: the annual Permanent Fund Dividend (PFD) counts as SNAP income and, if retained, as a resource — but a PFD Hold Harmless Program issues cash replacement payments to households who lose SNAP benefits because of it
supplements.text: Alaska's Permanent Fund Dividend, an annual payment issued to nearly all Alaska residents by the Department of Revenue, counts as unearned income to a SNAP household in the month received, and any retained PFD money counts as a countable resource in subsequent months. Alaska DOH's own live consumer page confirms, in two separate places (income treatment and resource treatment), that 'Special rules apply to Alaska Permanent Fund Dividends' without stating the mechanism in full. This pack located the fuller mechanism description in Alaska's legacy dpaweb.hss.state.ak.us manual (disclosed elsewhere in this pack as stale for dollar figures, last updated December 2021) and treats it as reasonably reliable for this ONE narrow, structural, non-dollar-figure feature because it describes a longstanding federal-waiver mechanism unlikely to have changed on the same cadence as annual COLA figures, and because it is cross-corroborated by the live consumer page's own PFD cross-references: Alaska has a federal waiver allowing SNAP cases to be suspended for up to four months (not necessarily consecutive, but within the PFD's fiscal year of July 1-June 30) when PFD income or retained PFD money would otherwise cause SNAP ineligibility or reduce a categorically-eligible household's allotment to zero; during suspension, DPA issues an equivalent PFD Hold Harmless cash payment instead, with no separate application required. One- and two-person households that would otherwise drop to the federal minimum SNAP benefit because of PFD income are also suspended and issued a Hold Harmless payment instead of the minimum benefit. A resident may also assign half of their PFD to the University of Alaska's 529 college-savings plan; the full pre-assignment PFD amount still counts as income to the person in whose name it is issued, the 529 funds themselves are an exempt resource, but any CASH REFUND later taken from that 529 plan counts as a non-recurring lump-sum resource and is explicitly NOT eligible for PFD Hold Harmless coverage. This pack flags this entire supplement as resting on a disclosed lower-confidence source (the legacy manual) for its mechanism-level detail, even though the live consumer page corroborates the mechanism's continued existence.

supplements.citation: Alaska DOH SNAP Subsistence Benefits guide (PDF, 2023)
supplements.heading: Alaska-only feature this pack found no equivalent for elsewhere in this roster: eligible households in limited-retail-access communities can use a specially designated SNAP ID card to buy subsistence hunting and fishing GEAR (not firearms or ammunition) with SNAP benefits
supplements.text: Alaska DOH's own SNAP Subsistence Benefits guide confirms a program this pack found no parallel for in any other state built in this roster: a household that (1) lives in a community where access to retail stores is difficult, AND (2) relies substantially on hunting and fishing for subsistence, may sign a subsistence hunting and fishing statement (drafted by the head of household, spouse, or authorized representative, filed at application, affirming the household intends to gather a majority portion of its food through subsistence hunting/fishing and does not intend the purchased items for commercial resale) and receive a specially designated SNAP ID card. That card may be used ONLY to purchase items necessary for attaining food: nets, lines, hooks, fishing rods, harpoons, knives, ice augers, and similar equipment — explicitly NOT firearms, ammunition, explosives, transportation items, clothing, or shelter. DOH's guide lists specific named communities (grouped Central/Coastal/Northern/Southeast) that are NOT considered to have limited retail access and are therefore presumptively ineligible for this program (e.g., Anchorage, Fairbanks, Juneau, Kenai, Kodiak, Sitka, Wasilla), while noting this list is not exhaustive and each request is evaluated case-by-case. This pack flags that its source PDF is dated 2023 and was not independently re-verified for FY2026-specific changes — this pack found no evidence the program has changed, but the specific ineligible-community list in particular could plausibly be updated without this pack having caught it.

supplements.citation: WebSearch corroboration (secondary, not independently fetched from a current USDA RMP state list)
supplements.heading: Alaska does NOT operate a Restaurant Meals Program
supplements.text: The Restaurant Meals Program (RMP) is a state OPTION under 7 CFR § 274.7(g) letting elderly (60+), disabled, and homeless SNAP recipients buy prepared, hot meals from authorized restaurants with EBT year-round. This pack found consistent corroboration that Alaska is not among the small group of states (AZ, CA, IL, MD, MA, MI, NY, RI, VA per this pack's most recent secondary-source check) that currently operate an RMP, and Alaska DOH's own consumer materials describe Quest Card use only at grocery stores and farmers markets, with no restaurant-purchase provision mentioned. This pack flags that its RMP-absence finding rests on secondary-source corroboration rather than a direct fetch of USDA's own current RMP state-operator list (which this pack did not independently re-fetch for Alaska specifically), and should be re-verified against a current primary USDA source before being restated with full confidence in a high-stakes context.

terms: how long does my snap approval last
supplements.citation: Alaska DOH SNAP consumer page (interim-report cadence); Alaska DOH ESAP page (36-month simplified certification)
supplements.heading: Alaska's SNAP certification periods run 12 or 24 months for most households (with a 6th- or 12th-month Interim Report respectively), and 36 months under the Elderly Simplified Application Project (ESAP) for all-elderly/disabled households
supplements.text: Alaska DOH's own consumer page describes the Interim Report cadence directly: 'if your household is certified to receive SNAP for 12 months, your Interim Report will be due in the 6th month, and if you're certified for 24 months, your Interim Report will be due the 12th month' — confirming Alaska uses both 12-month and 24-month standard certification periods, consistent with the national norm most of this roster's other states use. This pack did not locate a single DOH page stating the precise household-composition criteria that place a household on a 12-month versus 24-month track and flags this as a disclosed gap (a household should confirm its specific certification length directly with DPA rather than assume). Separately, Alaska offers the Elderly Simplified Application Project (ESAP) for households where all adults are age 60 or older or disabled — this pack confirms ESAP households receive a longer, 36-month certification period, a genuinely longer track than either the 12- or 24-month standard, reducing renewal burden specifically for Alaska's elderly/disabled population.
